methods.name: Stop-smoking medicine
methods.tagline: The biggest boost you can give yourself
methods.what: Licensed stop-smoking medicines (nicotine replacement, varenicline, cytisine, bupropion) raise long-term quit rates in hundreds of trials. Using one together with behavioural support works best of all. Nothing in this app comes close to that evidence.
methods.howTo: Ask a pharmacist, doctor or your national quitline which medicine suits you, and use it alongside the tools here.

methods.name: Get people on your side
methods.tagline: You do not have to do this alone
methods.what: Counselling from a trained adviser, in person or by phone, reliably raises quit rates, and proactive quitline calls help further. Free quitlines exist in most countries. Telling the people around you, and asking for specific help, is also part of standard stop-smoking support.
methods.howTo: Call or text your quitline today, and tell one person your quit date and how they can help.

methods.name: Rewards and money saved
methods.tagline: Watch what quitting puts back in your pocket
methods.what: A large Cochrane review found that rewards for staying smoke-free raise quit rates, and the effect lasted after rewards stopped. Those trials used real incentives for verified abstinence; tracking money saved and treating yourself is a related idea that has been tested far less.
methods.howTo: Pick a treat for day 1, week 1 and month 1, paid for from the money you are not spending on cigarettes.

methods.name: If-then plans
methods.tagline: Decide now what you will do when a trigger hits
methods.what: An if-then plan links a trigger to a set response, such as: if I finish dinner, then I get up and wash the dishes. A meta-analysis of 12 studies found these plans raised quit rates, but the studies were few and varied, so the true size of the benefit is uncertain.
methods.howTo: Write one plan for your strongest trigger: "If [situation], then I will [action]." Say it out loud once.

methods.name: Move your body
methods.tagline: A few minutes of movement can shrink a craving
methods.what: Pooled lab studies show that short bouts of activity, like a brisk walk, reliably lower cravings for a while. Adding exercise programmes to quit support has not been shown to raise long-term quit rates, so treat movement as a craving tool, not a cure.
methods.howTo: Right now, walk briskly, climb stairs or do squats for 5 to 10 minutes, then check how strong the urge is.

methods.name: Not a puff
methods.tagline: From quit day: not one puff, not one drag
methods.what: UK stop-smoking services teach a strict rule of no smoking at all after quit day. Studies of quitters find that most people who lapse go on to relapse, and the rule is linked to better results than cutting down. The evidence is mostly observational, not from trials of the rule itself.
methods.howTo: Treat "just one" as the start of smoking again. When the thought comes, say: not a puff.
methods.sourceName: NCSCT briefing: the 'not a puff' rule

methods.name: Text-message support
methods.tagline: Let regular messages keep you on track
methods.what: Automated text-message programmes raised quit rates compared with minimal support in a Cochrane review, and helped when added to other support. Evidence for smartphone apps on their own is still weak, including for apps like this one.
methods.howTo: Sign up for your country's free quit-by-text service if it has one; many quitlines offer it.

methods.name: Delay and distract
methods.tagline: Play a quick game while the urge passes
methods.what: Cravings usually fade within minutes. Small studies found that playing a visual puzzle game like Tetris for 3 minutes lowered craving strength, including for nicotine. These are small, short studies; they show cravings ease, not that games help people quit.
methods.howTo: Start a 3-minute game now. When it ends, rate your craving again.

methods.name: Slow breathing
methods.tagline: Slow your breath and let the urge settle
methods.what: In a small lab study, smokers who did a few minutes of controlled deep breathing had less craving and tension during abstinence. Other studies are mixed and the effects are small and short-lived, but it is free, safe and available anywhere.
methods.howTo: Breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds and out slowly for 6. Repeat 10 times.

methods.name: Urge surfing
methods.tagline: Ride the craving like a wave until it breaks
methods.what: Urge surfing means noticing a craving's feelings without acting on them, as it rises, peaks and falls. In one trial, students given brief instructions smoked less over the next week. A Cochrane review found no clear evidence that mindfulness programmes raise quit rates.
methods.howTo: Notice where you feel the urge in your body, describe it to yourself, and breathe with it until it passes.
methods.sourceName: Bowen & Marlatt 2009, Psychology of Addictive Behaviors

methods.name: Log your cravings
methods.tagline: Spot your triggers by writing them down
methods.what: Keeping track of when and where cravings hit is a standard part of stop-smoking support, and it helps you write better if-then plans. It has not been well tested on its own, so it is best seen as a helper for other methods.
methods.howTo: Each time a craving comes, log the time, place, mood and how strong it was from 1 to 10.
methods.sourceName: NHS Better Health: understand your triggers

methods.name: Your reasons
methods.tagline: Remind yourself what you gain by quitting
methods.what: Keeping your own reasons to hand is standard advice. One trial found that messages about the benefits of quitting led to more people staying quit than messages about the harms of smoking. That is a single study, so focusing on gains is a reasonable choice, not a proven one.
methods.howTo: Write three things you gain by quitting, like more money, easier breathing or time with family, and read them during a craving.
methods.sourceName: Toll et al. 2007, Psychology of Addictive Behaviors

methods.name: Bounce back from a slip
methods.tagline: A slip is a moment, not the end of your quit
methods.what: Relapse research describes an 'abstinence violation effect', where one slip leads to 'I've blown it' and giving up. One study found that confidence after a lapse mattered more than guilt. Being kind to yourself and getting straight back on track is sensible advice but has not been well tested.
methods.howTo: If you slip, throw the rest away, note what triggered it, make an if-then plan for next time, and carry on.

cravingFacts.text: The urge to smoke usually lasts only a few minutes.
cravingFacts.sourceName: National Cancer Institute, Clearing the Air

cravingFacts.text: Cravings pass, and riding one out does not cost you the progress you have made.
Even a short burst of activity can reduce the urge to smoke.
Withdrawal is usually strongest in the first week, especially the first 3 days.
On average, withdrawal symptoms ease within 3 to 4 weeks.
As time passes, cravings come further and further apart.
Withdrawal symptoms fade as long as you stay smoke-free.
Quitting at any age improves your health and can add up to a decade to your life.
Medicine plus support nearly doubles your chance of quitting compared with brief advice.

medication.summary: Cochrane reviews find that nicotine replacement therapy (patches, gum, lozenges, sprays) raises long-term quit rates by about 50 to 60%, bupropion by about 60%, and varenicline and cytisine roughly double the odds of quitting; using a patch together with a fast-acting form works better than one form alone. Combining any of these with behavioural support, such as counselling or a quitline, gives the best results of all, nearly doubling quit rates compared with brief advice. Not every medicine is available or suitable everywhere (cytisine is not sold in many countries), and some are not suitable in pregnancy or with certain health conditions. Talk to a pharmacist, doctor or quitline adviser to choose what is right for you; this app does not give dosing advice.
medication.sourceName: Cochrane 2023 component network meta-analysis (Lindson et al.)
